metadata.title: TMUA 2019 · Paper 2
metadata.description: Worked steps, progressive hints and reviewed follow-up questions.

matches.rationale: Selects powers from a multivariable product while retaining combination counts.
Collects a target coefficient through two selections, including numerical powers.
Accounts for both factors when selecting one target coefficient.
Converts a given linear factor into a coefficient equation.
Uses a known factor and subsequent division to recover polynomial roots.
Evaluates an unexpanded polynomial at a linear divisor zero using the remainder theorem.
Identifies the lost zero-factor case when cancellation removes solutions.
Tests which conclusions follow from simultaneous inequalities; rehearses disproof of an unsupported separate conclusion.
Checks that a counterexample satisfies the complete premise before rejecting the conclusion.
Selects the true-premise false-conclusion structure required for a counterexample.
Tests a particular composite number against three logically different number claims.
Tests both directions of divisibility expressed as an if-and-only-if condition.
Separates a square-product condition from an unjustified condition on each factor.
Finds the first unjustified inference from an equality of products.
Audits a chain of algebraic implications and finds an unjustified sign choice.
Identifies the point where squaring loses equivalence, rather than blaming a later consequence.
Checks eligible numerical values against both parts of a universal implication.
Counts integer counterexamples while checking antecedent truth and conclusion failure.

Both use supplied numerical data, checked against the complete permitted domain, to refute a quantified claim. The original repurposes a Pythagorean triple by rewriting a perfect-square base as a fourth power; the candidate evaluates root-and-power expressions at three supplied pairs. The common operations are exact power rewriting and a premise-true/conclusion-false counterexample test.
sharedKnowledge: Both use supplied numerical data, checked against the complete permitted domain, to refute a quantified claim. The original repurposes a Pythagorean triple by rewriting a perfect-square base as a fourth power; the candidate evaluates root-and-power expressions at three supplied pairs. The common operations are exact power rewriting and a premise-true/conclusion-false counterexample test.

matches.rationale: Audits inequality operations with potentially negative multipliers.
Tests invalid multiplication and division of inequalities by checking signs.
Finds the unjustified sign branch after a squared inequality.

Both translate a local neighbour requirement into coverage and justify attainable extremal arrangements. The seating question isolates circular coverage by occupied neighbours; the grid question first derives coverage by truthful neighbours, adds the prohibition on adjacent truthful cells and also asks for a maximum. This is a coverage prerequisite transfer, not the same full truth puzzle.
sharedKnowledge: Both translate a local neighbour requirement into coverage and justify attainable extremal arrangements. The seating question isolates circular coverage by occupied neighbours; the grid question first derives coverage by truthful neighbours, adds the prohibition on adjacent truthful cells and also asks for a maximum. This is a coverage prerequisite transfer, not the same full truth puzzle.

matches.rationale: Uses nonsquare parallelograms to separate geometric sufficient conditions.
Constructs a quadrilateral counterexample to an unjustified symmetry conclusion.
Tests an arithmetic-sum parity claim with allowed integer parameters.
Uses an AP sum condition without overclaiming the signs of individual terms.
Relates AP parity and median integrality, requiring the precise allowed cases.
Tracks trapezium-rule bias under graph transformations.
Uses reflection about an integration midpoint to compare integrals; isolates the symmetry part of the original.
Adds the exact rectangle created by a vertical shift; isolates the constant-height part of the error calculation.
Constructs a whole-function counterexample separating positive gradient from positive height.
Tests which function inequalities survive differentiation or integration.
sharedKnowledge: Tests which function inequalities survive differentiation or integration.

matches.rationale: Prerequisite transfer: separate derivative information from graph height, distinguish first from second derivative behaviour, and test necessity using a counterexample. The candidate applies second-derivative curvature to trapezium error rather than to endpoint derivative ordering.
Introduces a logarithmic variable and recovers original values after solving.
Combines simultaneous logarithmic relations, preserving positive argument restrictions.
Interprets a logarithm with the base as a variable; rehearses identifying the roles of base and argument.

Both derive an exact parameter restriction from a positive quadratic discriminant. The candidate additionally expresses the distance between the two formula roots and imposes strict bounds on that distance, instead of selecting a parameter-region diagram.
sharedKnowledge: Both derive an exact parameter restriction from a positive quadratic discriminant. The candidate additionally expresses the distance between the two formula roots and imposes strict bounds on that distance, instead of selecting a parameter-region diagram.

matches.rationale: Both impose a strictly positive discriminant for two distinct quadratic roots. The candidate extends that operation after u=x² by also requiring both transformed roots to be positive; it does not reproduce the original graphical parameter-region selection.
sharedKnowledge: Both impose a strictly positive discriminant for two distinct quadratic roots. The candidate extends that operation after u=x² by also requiring both transformed roots to be positive; it does not reproduce the original graphical parameter-region selection.

matches.rationale: Both translate if/iff options and eliminate an option if it forces another option, under an exactly-one-true premise. The candidate adds contrapositive equivalences of sign rules; the original also uses containment of threshold premise sets.
sharedKnowledge: Both translate if/iff options and eliminate an option if it forces another option, under an exactly-one-true premise. The candidate adds contrapositive equivalences of sign rules; the original also uses containment of threshold premise sets.

matches.rationale: Both keep logical dependencies between whole statements while testing a consistent truth assignment. The candidate adds self-referential truth counts and an unknown name fact; it practises the consistency step rather than threshold containment.
sharedKnowledge: Both keep logical dependencies between whole statements while testing a consistent truth assignment. The candidate adds self-referential truth counts and an unknown name fact; it practises the consistency step rather than threshold containment.

matches.rationale: Both impose exactly one true statement and reject cases that force multiple truths. The candidate evaluates five finite labels at a common positive integer; the original compares universal if/iff statements over nested input sets. This transfers the truth-dependency check rather than the same numerical calculation.
sharedKnowledge: Both impose exactly one true statement and reject cases that force multiple truths. The candidate evaluates five finite labels at a common positive integer; the original compares universal if/iff statements over nested input sets. This transfers the truth-dependency check rather than the same numerical calculation.

matches.rationale: Proves a universal inequality and refutes competing bounds using allowed points. This strengthens the all-input proof step rather than repeating the parameter/modulus setup.
Tests a universal real-variable claim using inputs designed to defeat a proposed parameter condition.
Converts modulus constraints into regions and proves an endpoint extreme attainable; trains the modulus-range prerequisite.

Both bound positive surd quantities against exact rational benchmarks before selecting the correct real branch or comparison. The original uses those sign checks when recognising nested radicals as squares. The candidate bounds a power of sqrt(2) minus one and compares it with other exact values; it does not teach the original binomial-square recognition.
sharedKnowledge: compare positive surds by squaring positive bounds
check the sign and size of a radical expression before using it

matches.rationale: Both simplify positive surd expressions exactly and establish their signs before selecting a principal root or comparing a reciprocal. The original recognises binomial squares under radicals; the candidate rationalises or bounds a surd denominator within a mixed-number comparison. This is the sign-and-surd prerequisite, not the full nested-root method.
sharedKnowledge: simplify surd expressions without decimal approximation
justify positivity before taking reciprocals or principal roots

matches.rationale: Both simplify sums involving principal square roots while preserving the nonnegative branch. The candidate uses a squared sum and Vieta relations; the original recognises exact squared surd forms.
sharedKnowledge: Square a sum with its cross term

matches.rationale: Recognises equivalent reflection identities by renaming the universal input.
Applies reflection and translation in order and tracks the resulting input and output.
Composes translation, reflection and scaling while preserving their stated order.

scopeNotes: Q9 has no other exact circular-seating coverage problem in the archive: its links practise exhaustive arrangements and proving an attained extremum.
Q12 has no three distinct exact event-inclusion ordering questions: its links practise rigorous interpretation of events, symmetry and sampling restrictions.
Q13 has one separate close trapezium-error problem; the other links isolate reflection and constant-shift knowledge.
2019 P2 Q2 is reprinted as 2020 P1 Q2. The latter is excluded as a follow-up, despite having a different source ID.
The official Q14 worked-answer page has derivative-symbol and inequality-direction typos. The authored solution instead verifies explicit quadratic and cubic counterexamples by differentiation.
